vignette: The sun breaks over the ridge at 0400, and Kwame is already awake before his alarm. At forty-six, he still measures his days in watch periods, in the heavy space between silence and sudden noise. Twelve years ago, in a valley he never names to his wife, the ground turns to shrapnel. He remembers the taste of copper, the jam of his rifle bolt, the wet thud of his squad leader hitting the dirt beside him. He crawls through dust and cordite, hands shaking so violently he can barely grip the edge of an armored door. He survives. He comes home. But the body he returns in never fully unpacks. He and his wife, Amara, built a life in the quiet eastern highlands, far from the coastal cities that always feel too loud, too crowded. She knows the cadence of his breathing when he sleeps. She knows not to startle him when he jolts upright, her hands hovering before she pulls the blanket to his shoulders. They have learned the architecture of his silence. They love each other, but the love sits beside the weight, not on top of it. Kwame works as a park ranger, tracking elephant migrations and monitoring water levels across a private nature reserve. The job suits him in some ways: the steady rhythm of boots on laterite soil, the predictable call of morning birds, the open sky that demands observation rather than engagement. Yet the work pulls at him daily. When a branch snaps too loud behind him, his hand goes instinctively to where his sidearm used to hang. He checks the perimeter fence twice before leaving the station. He avoids the radio broadcast that plays at the mess hall, switches it off the moment he hears distant gunfire in a news segment, changes the dial with a sharp, practiced click. At night, the wind moving through the acacia groves sounds like rotors. He wakes at the edge of sleep, heart hammering against his ribs, certain that the perimeter has been breached. He lies there until dawn, counting breaths, waiting for the panic to settle into a familiar ache behind his eyes. He tells himself it is just the dry season, the heat, the altitude. His muscles know better. In his truck, parked along a fire road at the reserve's edge, Kwame watches the afternoon light bleach the asphalt. He thinks about the last patrol, when the ranger radio crackled with static and his jaw tightened until it ached. He told himself it was equipment malfunction, but his body remembered forward observers, the urgency in clipped calls. He drives further out, away from the station, away from the conversations that pile up at the mess hall. He prefers the company of the old game trails, where the silence feels earned rather than imposed. Amara leaves a cup of tea on the desk in his office. It goes cold while he stares at a topographic map, tracing contour lines that mirror the ridgelines of that valley. She asks him about his weekend, and he gives her a summary of water levels and camera trap footage, careful to leave out the way his chest tightened when a helicopter passed overhead last Tuesday. They sit together in the evening, watching the sky shift from blue to iron. He notices how he flinches when she reaches for his hand in the car, how he sits rigid in crowded rooms, how he has stopped volunteering for the annual veterans' gathering because the smell of burning rubber drags him back to the road he crawled out of. The afternoon shifts toward gold. Kwame starts the truck's engine, the sputter sending a fresh jolt through his shoulders. He shifts into gear, eyes scanning the treeline, then forcing them back to the road. He turns the radio off. He drives toward the ranger station, past the grazing wildebeest, past the rusted fuel cans from a decade ago, past the man he was when the world narrowed to a crosshair and the next second. He parks beside his desk, sets his radio on the passenger seat, and steps out into the cool evening air. The birds are coming back. He listens to them.
